series.name: Second Shift
series.tagline: Your day job pays the bills. Your second shift pays the soul.
series.concept: People's secret lives after 6 PM. A banker does stand-up. A CA paints. An auto driver writes screenplays. Each episode follows one person's double life — the 'respectable' day job and the 'impractical' night passion — all set in a Pune co-working space run by a retired IAS officer named Rajan.

episodes.title: The Punchline

slides.text: Meera Joshi has approved 3,000 loan applications in four years. She knows every RBI guideline by heart. Her colleagues call her 'the rule book.' By day, she's the most serious person on the 7th floor of HDFC Bank, Koregaon Park branch.

But every Tuesday and Thursday at 9:30 PM, Meera walks into a basement bar in Koregaon Park. She picks up a mic. And she makes 40 strangers laugh about the absurdity of banking. Her best bit? 'My bank rejected a loan for a guy who wanted to open a comedy club. I felt personally attacked.'

She started comedy after a panic attack in the office bathroom. Three years of saying 'as per guidelines' had turned her into a robot. A friend dragged her to an open mic. She watched. Went back. Watched again. Third time, she signed up. Bombed completely. Felt more alive than she had in years.

She found Second Shift six months ago. Rajan's co-working space, open from 7 PM to 2 AM. She books Desk 4 every Tuesday to write new material. The CA at Desk 7 sometimes overhears her mumbling punchlines and tries not to laugh. He fails every time.

Tonight she's testing a new five-minute set. It's about Aadhaar cards. 'The government gave us a 12-digit identity. But what if your real identity doesn't fit in 12 digits?' The auto driver at Desk 12 looks up from his screenplay. 'Bhai, that's my entire movie plot,' he says. They both laugh.

Last week, a colleague shared a reel in the office group chat. A comedian riffing about RBI guidelines. The camera was shaky, the face wasn't clear. 'This person really gets banking,' her manager wrote. Meera's heart stopped. Then she typed: 'Haha, so true.' She's never performed at that venue again.
Rajan watches from the counter, wiping a chai glass. 'Log kehte hain comedy easy hai. Asli joke toh yeh hai ki duniya chahti hai tum ek hi cheez bano.'

episodes.synopsis: Meera Joshi, compliance officer at HDFC Bank by day, does stand-up comedy at open mics by night. She's terrified her branch manager will find out.
episodes.caption: She makes 40 strangers laugh every week. But she can't tell a single colleague. What's the thing YOU do that nobody at work knows about?

episodes.title: Canvas and Compliance

slides.text: Vikram Desai has audited companies worth 200 crores. His Excel sheets are legendary — color-coded, formula-perfect, zero errors. At Deloitte Pune, they call him 'the machine.' He hasn't taken a sick day in three years.

At 8 PM, Vikram opens a different kind of file. Acrylics. Canvas. Turpentine. He paints abstract cityscapes — Pune at 2 AM, Mumbai locals in monsoon, Varanasi ghats at dawn. He sells them on Instagram under the name 'Neelkanth.' No face. No real name. 47 paintings sold. His clients must never know.

His father was a painter. Died broke. Vikram promised his mother he'd never pick up a brush. He kept that promise for 15 years. Then one Diwali, alone in his flat, he bought a canvas from a roadside stall. 'Just to try,' he told himself. He painted till 4 AM. Called in sick for the first time ever.

He comes to Second Shift because his flat is too small and the smell of turpentine bothers the neighbors. Desk 7, next to the window. He lays out a plastic sheet, sets up his portable easel, and disappears into color. Meera at Desk 4 mumbles punchlines. He catches every third one and laughs. She doesn't know he's the one buying her chai.

Tonight, a notification. 'Neelkanth, your painting of the Pune rain was featured on ArtStation India's weekly picks.' 23,000 views. His hands are shaking. This is the most people who've ever seen his work. More than any audit report. And not a single one knows his real name.

A junior at Deloitte walks into the space. She's there to use the printer. She sees the painting. 'Oh wow, this is beautiful. Who are you?' Vikram freezes. 'I'm... just renting the desk.' She takes a photo of the painting. 'My boss would love this. He's really into art.' Her boss is Vikram's audit partner.
Rajan places a chai next to the easel. 'Tum audit mein risk calculate karte ho. Par asli risk toh yeh hai — apni painting pe apna naam na likh paana.'

episodes.synopsis: Vikram Desai, chartered accountant at a Big 4 firm, paints at night and sells anonymously online. He's terrified his clients will Google him and find color instead of columns.
episodes.caption: He audits companies worth crores by day. By night, he paints cities he's never shown his face in. What would YOU create if nobody knew it was you?

episodes.title: 14 Scripts

slides.text: Farhan Sheikh drives auto number MH-12-AB-7734. He knows every shortcut in Pune. Swargate to Hinjewadi in 40 minutes, even during peak traffic. His passengers rate him 4.8 stars on Ola. They don't know about the notebook under his seat.

14 screenplays. Three comedies, four thrillers, two family dramas, five 'experimental' — whatever that means. All written in a mix of Hindi and Marathi. All sitting in a blue plastic folder in his auto's storage box. He's sent two to production houses. One got a 'we'll get back to you.' That was three years ago.

He grew up watching Doordarshan in a one-room house in Latur. His mother cleaned houses. His father drove a tempo. Every night, they'd watch whatever was on TV. Farhan didn't just watch — he'd rewrite the endings. 'Agar main writer hota, toh heroine ko bachata.' He was eight. He's been rewriting the world since.

At Second Shift, Farhan types his scripts into Google Docs. The security guard — Pratap — taught him the basics of using a laptop. In return, Farhan reads his scripts aloud to Pratap during chai breaks. Pratap's feedback is brutal. 'Interval point weak hai, bhai.' Farhan rewrites it. Every single time.

Tonight, the college student at Desk 2 — Ananya, the podcast girl — overhears Farhan reading dialogue aloud. She walks over. 'What is this?' 'Script hai. Number 14.' She reads two pages. Then ten. Then thirty. 'Can I read this on my podcast? Like a radio play?' Farhan doesn't speak for six seconds. Then: 'Haan.'

Three weeks later, Ananya's podcast episode drops. 'Auto Waale Farhan Ki Kahaani' — she reads his script with two voice actors. 14,000 listens in a week. Farhan plays it in his auto on loop. A passenger asks, 'Kya sun rahe ho?' He says, 'Bas ek story.' He doesn't say it's his. Not yet.
Rajan overhears and shakes his head smiling. 'Duniya kehti hai auto chalao. Par iska auto bhi kahaani hai — bas kisi ne padhi nahi thi.'

episodes.synopsis: Farhan Sheikh, auto rickshaw driver in Pune, has written 14 full screenplays in five years. He writes at Second Shift from 10 PM to 1 AM. Tonight, someone actually reads one.
episodes.caption: 14 scripts. Not one produced. Until a college girl with a podcast said 'can I read this?' Sometimes your big break comes from Desk 2. Whose work are you sleeping on — maybe your own?

episodes.title: Bull Run

slides.text: Sunita Agarwal makes the best dal baati in Aundh. Her husband's friends say so every Sunday. She manages a house, two kids, a mother-in-law, and a husband who thinks women and money don't mix. By 6 PM, dinner is served, kids are studied, and Sunita's 'day job' is done.

At 7:30 PM, after everyone's eaten, Sunita tells her husband she's going for 'kitty party practice.' She walks to Second Shift. Desk 9. Opens Zerodha on her laptop. She started with 50,000 from her savings — money her mother gave her. That 50,000 is now 8.7 lakhs. In eleven months.

Her husband once said at a dinner party: 'Sunita doesn't understand money. She just spends it.' Everyone laughed. Sunita laughed too. She went home, downloaded Zerodha, and spent three months watching every Varsity module. She understood money just fine. She just never had permission to touch it.

At Second Shift, nobody asks why a housewife is reading candlestick charts at 10 PM. The auto driver Farhan once asked her for stock tips. She said, 'Tata Motors — hold for six months.' He put in 5,000. It's at 8,200 now. He brings her chai every night as thanks.

Tonight, a trade she's been watching for two weeks finally triggers. Bajaj Finance, 2% jump in after-hours. She'd placed the order at 3 PM from her kitchen while making rotis. Profit: 34,000 in one trade. She screenshots it. Saves it in a hidden folder on her phone called 'Recipes.'

Her husband's financial advisor comes for dinner. He mentions a stock. 'Bajaj Finance is overvalued,' he says confidently. Sunita almost says, 'I made 34,000 on it yesterday.' She bites her tongue. Her mother-in-law asks, 'Sunita, aur chai laaogi?' She goes to the kitchen. Smiles. Pours the chai.
Rajan glances at her screen as he walks by. He doesn't understand the charts. But he understands the smile. 'Agar Sunita ji stock market samjha dein toh IAS ki exam bhi nikal lein.'

episodes.synopsis: Sunita Agarwal, housewife from a traditional Marwari family, secretly day-trades from her phone and now from Second Shift. Her portfolio outperforms her husband's financial advisor.
episodes.caption: She makes dal baati for dinner. Then she makes 34,000 on Bajaj Finance. Her portfolio is in a folder called 'Recipes.' What's YOUR hidden folder?

episodes.title: The Man Behind the Counter

slides.text: Everyone at Second Shift knows Rajan as the uncle who makes great chai and never judges. He opens the space at 7 PM, closes at 2 AM, and knows everyone's order by heart. Meera gets cutting chai, Vikram gets black coffee, Farhan gets double sugar. Nobody's asked what Rajan did before this.

Tonight, a young man walks in. Government lanyard still around his neck. He freezes when he sees Rajan. 'Sir? Rajan Kulkarni sir? Pune collector wale?' The space goes quiet. Meera looks up from her notebook. Vikram's brush stops mid-stroke. Rajan wipes the counter. 'Yahan sirf Rajan hai. Chai peeni hai?'

Rajan Kulkarni. IAS, 1989 batch. District collector twice. Secretary-level postings in Delhi. 30 years of transfers, files, red tape, and power. He retired three years ago. His colleagues threw a party. He left early. Went home and stared at the ceiling for two months.

He found this space — an old printing press in Kothrud — while walking one night. The landlord wanted to demolish it. Rajan signed a lease the next day. 'Main 30 saal woh kaam kiya jo karna tha. Ab woh jagah bana raha hoon jahaan log woh karein jo karna chahte hain.' Second Shift opened four months later.

The young government clerk sits at Desk 1. He's brought a laptop. He opens a music production software. 'Sir, I make lo-fi beats at night,' he says to Rajan. 'Nobody in the collectorate knows.' Rajan smiles. 'Toh sahi jagah aaye ho.' He pours him chai. No more questions.

Later, Meera asks Rajan quietly: 'IAS the aap? Collector the?' Rajan looks at the space — Vikram painting, Farhan typing, Sunita on her charts, the new clerk making beats. He says, 'Collector tha. Log mujhse darte the. Yahan log mujhe chai ke liye thanks bolte hain. Batao kya better hai.'
Rajan locks up at 2 AM. Walks past his old nameplate — he keeps it in the drawer under the counter. 'Rajan Kulkarni, IAS.' He closes the drawer. Opens the door for tomorrow.

episodes.synopsis: Rajan's backstory. A young government clerk recognizes him as the IAS officer who once ran the district. Rajan brushes it off. But the space learns something about its owner.
episodes.caption: 30 years as an IAS officer. Now he makes chai for people chasing their dreams at midnight. Respect isn't about titles — it's about what you build after them. What would you do after your 'real job' ends?

episodes.title: Too Late

slides.text: Priya Nair writes code that processes 2 million transactions a day. She's a senior developer at Infosys, Hinjewadi. Standups at 10 AM, sprint reviews on Friday, Jira tickets that never end. Her LinkedIn says 'passionate about technology.' It's not wrong. It's just not the whole truth.

At 28, Priya walked into a Bharatanatyam class. The teacher looked at her feet, then her face. 'You should have started at 6.' Priya said, 'I know. Can I start at 28?' She's been dancing for two years now. Her anklets are in her laptop bag. Always.

Her mother danced. Performed at temples in Kerala. Then married, moved to Pune, and never danced again. Priya found her mother's old anklets in a trunk after she passed. She tried them on. They fit. She cried for an hour. Then she searched 'Bharatanatyam classes near me.'

Second Shift has a small open area near the back — no desks, just floor. Rajan cleared it when Priya asked if she could practice. She dances from midnight to 1:30 AM, when the space is quietest. The security guard Pratap watches sometimes. He says nothing. Just nods. Once, he clapped. She nearly cried again.

Tonight, the HR manager — Kavya, the tattoo artist — asks Priya: 'Can I sketch you while you dance? For a tattoo design.' Priya dances. Kavya sketches. By 1 AM, there's a drawing of a dancer in mid-flight. 'This could be on someone's skin forever,' Kavya says. 'Your mother's anklets, someone's arm.' Priya stares at the drawing.

A colleague from Infosys sees her Instagram story — a 3-second clip of ghungroo bells, no face shown. He DMs her: 'Is that you? Didn't know you danced!' She types three different replies. Deletes all of them. Then posts another story — this time, her feet, mid-step, anklets shining. Caption: 'Started at 28. Still starting.' 47 likes. She doesn't delete it.
Rajan sweeps the dance floor after she leaves. 'Log kehte hain der ho gayi. Par der tab hoti hai jab shuru hi na karo.'

episodes.synopsis: Priya Nair, software engineer at Infosys, started learning Bharatanatyam at 28. Everyone said it was too late. She dances at Second Shift after midnight.
episodes.caption: Her mother danced in temples. She dances in a co-working space at midnight. They told her she started too late. She's still starting. What have you been told is 'too late' for?

episodes.title: Hello World

slides.text: Pratap Gaikwad stands at Gate 3 of Seasons Society, Magarpatta, from 7 AM to 7 PM. He checks visitor IDs, lifts the boom barrier, and says 'good morning sir' 200 times a day. He's 24. He's been doing this for three years. The residents don't know his last name.

Every night at 11 PM, Pratap opens a second-hand laptop at Desk 11. He's learning Python. He found freeCodeCamp on YouTube six months ago. He's completed 40% of the course. He keeps a notebook — every error, every fix, every small victory. Page 1 says: 'print("hello world") — this is where it starts.'

He's from Beed. His father is a farmer. Pratap came to Pune to send money home. Security guard was the first job he got. But every day, he watches the IT people in his society go to work — laptops in hand, Swiggy orders for lunch, Uber home at night. He thought, 'They learned something. I can learn too. Just not during the day.'

Priya noticed him one night, stuck on a loop error. She looked at his screen. 'Yahan colon lagao.' He stared at her. 'Aap engineer ho?' 'Haan. Aur dancer. Dono.' Now she teaches him every Saturday from 11 PM to 1 AM. He calls her 'ma'am.' She says 'Priya bol.' He still says ma'am.

Tonight, Pratap builds his first program without help. A simple calculator. It works. He runs it five times to make sure. Then he turns the laptop to show Farhan. 'Dekh, maine banaya.' Farhan types in 7 x 7. The answer comes: 49. 'Bhai,' Farhan says, 'mere 14 scripts ka budget calculate kar de.' They both crack up.

A resident from his society comes to Second Shift for a meeting. Sees Pratap at a laptop, coding. Does a double take. 'Pratap? Gate 3 Pratap?' Pratap looks up. He doesn't shrink. For the first time, he says: 'Haan. Gate 3 Pratap. Jo coding seekh raha hai.' The resident says nothing. Then: 'Need any help? I'm in IT.'
Rajan watches from behind the counter. Wipes his eyes quickly. 'Yeh space isi ke liye banaya tha.'

episodes.synopsis: Pratap Gaikwad, security guard at a Magarpatta housing society by day, learns coding at Second Shift from 11 PM to 2 AM. Priya the dancer-engineer teaches him on weekends.
episodes.caption: He opens gates for a living. Now he's opening a terminal. Gate 3 Pratap is learning to code. Who decides what you're 'supposed' to do? Not a uniform. Not a job title.

episodes.title: Once Upon a Clause

slides.text: Rohit Mehta reviews merger agreements worth 500 crores. He's a senior associate at AZB & Partners, Pune office. He uses words like 'notwithstanding,' 'hereinafter,' and 'force majeure' before lunch. His clients think he's sharp, cold, precise. He wears suits that cost more than most bookshelves.

At 9 PM, Rohit opens a different document. 'The Adventures of Chunnu the Cloud.' A children's book about a cloud who's scared of thunder. He's written four books. All unpublished. All illustrated by him — yes, the merger lawyer draws clouds with faces and suns wearing sunglasses.

His niece is five. She asked him to tell her a story. He told her about Chunnu the Cloud. She listened for 40 minutes without moving. Then she said, 'Rohit mama, you should write this down.' A five-year-old gave him more career direction than his entire law firm. He started writing that night.

At Second Shift, Desk 6. He writes from 9 PM to midnight. Meera at Desk 4 was reading over his shoulder one night — she thought he was working on a contract. She saw a cloud with a face. She laughed so hard she knocked over her chai. Now she proofreads every chapter. 'Rohit, the frog should definitely be a CA. Trust me.'

Tonight, Rohit finishes Book 5. 'Chunnu and the Monsoon.' Meera reads the ending aloud in her comedy voice. Vikram the painter looks over and says, 'I'll illustrate it professionally if you want. For free.' Rohit stares. 'You paint?' 'You write children's books?' They both laugh. Nobody is who they seem here.

A colleague texts Rohit a screenshot. 'Bro, look at this children's book page someone shared on Twitter. Reminds me of your niece.' It's Rohit's illustration. Meera had posted it on her comedy page — 'Even clouds have anxiety' — without telling him. 4,000 likes. Rohit's phone nearly slips. He texts Meera: 'Kya kiya tune?' She replies: 'Stand-up nahi, toh publishing kar diya.'
Rajan places three chai cups on the desk. Looks at the cloud drawing on screen. 'Badal bhi darta hai. Par baarish toh wahi laata hai.'

episodes.synopsis: Advocate Rohit Mehta, corporate lawyer at a top Pune firm, writes children's books in secret. Meera the comedian discovers his manuscripts and can't stop reading.
episodes.caption: A 500-crore merger lawyer who draws clouds with faces. His niece gave him better career advice than his firm ever did. What would a five-year-old tell you to do?

episodes.title: Frequency

slides.text: Nisha Sharma teaches Class 10 math at DPS Kothrud. Quadratic equations, trigonometry, probability. She's the teacher who stays back to explain things twice. Students rate her 'strict but fair.' She wears salwar kameez to school and sensible footwear. The vice principal approves.

On Friday and Saturday nights, 'N.Hz' plays at a basement club in Koregaon Park. EDM, lo-fi, Bollywood remixes. She built her DJ setup from a second-hand controller and free software. Her mixing is mathematical — BPM transitions, harmonic keys, perfectly timed drops. Turns out, math and music are the same language.

She grew up in Indore listening to her brother's EDM collection on a shared computer. He went into IT. She became a teacher — 'stable job, good for marriage.' She taught for six years without touching music. Then one night, she heard a track in a cafe and felt her fingers move like they were on a controller. She bought one the next day. Didn't tell anyone.

At Second Shift, Desk 3 with headphones. She practices mixes Wednesday through Thursday. The lo-fi clerk from Episode 5 — Arjun — sometimes plugs in and they do back-to-back. A math teacher and a government clerk making music at 11 PM in a co-working space. Rajan has stopped being surprised.

Tonight, the club owner calls. 'N.Hz, I want you for the Saturday residency. Monthly. Paid.' Nisha's first paid gig. She does the math — it's less than one month's teaching salary. But it's not about the money. It's about someone saying: 'Your sound is good enough to pay for.' She says yes before he finishes the sentence.

Monday morning. A student shows her a reel. 'Ma'am, look at this DJ. She's so cool.' It's Nisha. The video is dark, face not clear, but the controller and the hands are visible. Nisha's heart stops. She watches herself on a student's phone. 'Haan, achha hai,' she says calmly. The student moves on. Nisha's hands are shaking under the desk.
Rajan adjusts his hearing aid. 'Mujhe music samajh nahi aata. Par main itna jaanta hoon — jo cheez tumhe aadhi raat tak jaaga rakhe, woh tumhari calling hai.'

episodes.synopsis: Nisha Sharma, math teacher at a CBSE school in Kothrud, DJs under the name 'N.Hz' at small clubs on weekends. She practices mixing at Second Shift.
episodes.caption: She teaches trigonometry by day and drops beats by night. Turns out, math and music are the same thing — patterns, timing, and knowing when to let go. What's your hidden frequency?

episodes.title: The Offer

slides.text: It's a Wednesday night. The space is full. Meera's writing jokes, Vikram's painting, Farhan's typing, Sunita's on her charts. Normal night. Then a white Innova parks outside. A man in a safari suit walks in with two assistants carrying files. Everyone looks up. Rajan doesn't.

'Rajan ji, I'm from the municipal corporation. We've heard about your space. Very impressive. We want to help — a small grant, some publicity, maybe a board with the commissioner's photo.' He slides a form across the counter. Rajan reads it in three seconds. He's written a hundred forms like this.

'Clause 4 — the corporation can use the space for official events. Clause 7 — approval required for any activity after 11 PM. Clause 12 — the corporation's name on all branding.' Rajan puts the form down. 'Yeh help nahi hai. Yeh control hai. Main jaanta hoon. Maine 30 saal yeh kiya hai.'

The official's smile falters. 'Rajan ji, aap samajh nahi rahe —' 'Main bahut achhe se samajh raha hoon. Main IAS tha. Maine yeh offers khud bheje hain. Grant dete hain, phir jagah apni ho jaati hai. Yahan ke logon ko safe space chahiye, sarkari event venue nahi.'

The official leaves. His Innova's diesel engine rumbles away. The space exhales. Meera breaks the silence: 'Rajan uncle, aap IAS the aur aapne usse aise bhagaya?' Rajan goes back to wiping the counter. 'IAS tha isliye bhagaya. Unki language mujhe aati hai.'

Later, Sunita walks up to the counter. 'Rajan ji, space ka rent kitna hai? If there's a shortfall, I have some... savings.' She means her trading profits. Farhan joins: 'Main bhi help karunga.' Then Vikram. Then Priya. Then Pratap. Rajan looks at them. 'Abhi toh koi problem nahi hai.' 'Haan,' says Meera, 'par family toh pehle se ready rehti hai.'
Rajan pours six chai cups. Hands trembling slightly. 'Sarkaar mein 30 saal kaam kiya. Kisi ne chai nahi pucha. Yahan rent pooch rahe hain.' He smiles. 'Yeh jagah bach gayi. Aaj nahi, har roz.'

episodes.synopsis: A municipal official visits Second Shift, offering to 'support' the space with government funding. Rajan sees through it instantly — he used to be on the other side of that table.
episodes.caption: The government offered help. Rajan knew it wasn't help. When you've been inside the system, you see the strings. Sometimes protecting a space means saying no to power. What would you protect?

episodes.title: Rewired

slides.text: Dr. Aarav Patil has performed 600 knee replacements. His hands are steady, his diagnoses precise. Sahyadri Hospital, Deccan. Patients wait two months for his appointment. He's everything his parents wanted — a doctor. Respected. Settled. Successful. He feels like a fraud every single day.

His bedroom closet has a false back. Behind his suits — Arduino boards, servo motors, 3D-printed parts, and a half-built robotic arm. He started in secret two years ago. YouTube tutorials first, then courses, then building. The arm can now pick up a chai cup. It's not much. It's everything.

AIEEE 2009. Rank 3,400. IIT Bombay, mechanical engineering, seat confirmed. His father said: 'Doctor bano. Engineer toh har galli mein hai.' Aarav argued for a week. Lost. Took NEET. Got into medical college. Became what they wanted. The IIT acceptance letter is still in his drawer. He's never thrown it away.

Second Shift gives him what his closet can't — space. Desk 10, with extra power outlets. Rajan didn't blink when Aarav walked in with a box of circuits. 'Pehle ek doctor aata tha jo gaana gaata tha. Ab ek robot banata hai. Koi problem nahi.' Pratap the security-guard-coder helps him with the programming. A surgeon and a guard, debugging together at midnight.

Tonight, the arm works. Fully. Aarav programs it to pick up a chai cup from the counter and bring it to Desk 10. It wobbles, hesitates, then delivers. The whole space watches. Farhan starts clapping. Then everyone does. Aarav stares at his creation — the thing his 17-year-old self wanted to build.

His father visits Pune. Comes to the hospital. 'Beta, proud of you.' Aarav almost says it. Almost says 'Papa, I build robots at night.' Instead he says, 'Thanks, Papa.' On the drive home, his father says, 'Achha kiya doctor bane. Engineering mein kya rakha tha.' Aarav grips the steering wheel. Says nothing. Goes to Second Shift at 11 PM.
Rajan hands him chai. 'Tumhare papa ne doctor banaya. Tumne khud ko engineer banaya. Dono sach hain. Dono tum ho.'

episodes.synopsis: Dr. Aarav Patil, orthopedic surgeon at Sahyadri Hospital, builds robots at Second Shift. His parents forced medicine. He wanted engineering. Now he's building what he always dreamed of.
episodes.caption: 600 knee replacements by day. A robotic arm that carries chai by night. His IIT acceptance letter is still in his drawer. Some dreams don't expire. What's still in YOUR drawer?

episodes.title: Under the Skin

slides.text: Kavya Rao writes policies about 'acceptable appearance standards' at TechMahindra. She's drafted the dress code. She's enforced the 'no visible tattoos during client meetings' rule. She's sat in meetings where someone said 'tattoos are unprofessional' and she nodded. She has 11 tattoos. All hidden under formal wear.

At 9 PM, the blazer comes off. Kavya's arms tell stories — a compass on her left wrist, a lotus on her forearm, geometric patterns climbing her shoulder. She's been tattooing for three years. Started on practice skin from Amazon. Then friends. Then friends of friends. Now she has a waiting list. All under the name 'KR Ink.' No one at TechMahindra knows.

Her first tattoo was at 19. A small bird on her ankle. Her father didn't speak to her for a month. Her mother cried. 'Log kya kahenge?' Kavya learned two things that month: tattoos are permanent, and so is her love for them. She just learned to hide both.

Rajan gave her the back corner — Desk 14, near the washroom, extra bright light. She set up a small station. Second Shift regulars line up. She's tattooed Priya's mother's anklets on her wrist. Farhan got his auto number on his forearm. Even Sunita got one — a tiny bull, hidden behind her ear. 'For my portfolio,' Sunita said. 'The bull market one,' she whispered.

Tonight, Rajan sits in her chair. 'Mujhe bhi ek chahiye.' The space goes silent. Rajan wants a tattoo. 'Kya likhwana hai?' Kavya asks. He thinks. 'Permission.' One word. On his wrist. She inks it in clean, simple letters. The retired IAS officer gets his first tattoo at 63. The space erupts.

A TechMahindra colleague DMs KR Ink's Instagram: 'Hey, I want a tattoo but I work in corporate. Can you do it somewhere hidden? My HR is strict about visible ink.' Kavya reads the message three times. The HR is strict. The HR is her. She books the appointment. Wears a mask. Does the tattoo. Her colleague never knows who inked her.
Rajan looks at his wrist. The ink is fresh. It stings a little. He smiles. 'Ab jab koi poochega ki yeh space kyun banaya — main bas yeh dikha doonga.'

episodes.synopsis: Kavya Rao, HR manager at a Pune IT company, is a tattoo artist at night. She works from Second Shift, inking people who come in after hours.
episodes.caption: She writes the dress code by day. She breaks it by night. She tattooed her own colleague without them knowing. And Rajan got his first tattoo at 63. One word: 'Permission.' What would YOUR tattoo say?

episodes.title: Softly, Soldier

slides.text: Colonel Suresh Rawat served 28 years in the Indian Army. Three field postings, two commendations, one shrapnel scar on his left arm. He retired at 54. His neighbors still call him 'Colonel sahab.' He wakes at 5 AM, irons his own clothes, and keeps his shoes polished. Old habits. The army never really leaves.

At 8 PM, Colonel Rawat puts on an apron. Pink. With flowers. His wife bought it as a joke. He wears it with the same discipline as his uniform. He bakes — red velvet, black forest, custom fondant. His piping is military-precise. His layering is architectural. He's doing 500 orders a month now. Instagram handle: @MessTinBakes.

During a posting in Leh, the mess cook fell sick. Rawat was the only one who knew how to bake — his mother had taught him. He made a chocolate cake for 40 soldiers. They loved it. Then someone found out and the jokes started. 'Colonel sahab, aaj kya bana rahe ho — bunker ya bundt cake?' He laughed along. He stopped baking for 15 years.

Second Shift has a small kitchen — originally for chai. Rajan let him expand it. Now there's an oven, a mixer, and a cooling rack. Rawat bakes from 8 PM to midnight. The whole space smells like vanilla by 9. Nobody complains. Meera says, 'My comedy writing is 30% better when it smells like cake.' Rawat always saves her a slice.

Tonight, a wedding order. Five-tier cake. The biggest he's done. He's been planning it for two weeks — sketches, flavor profiles, structural calculations. 'A cake this big is basically engineering,' Aarav the robot-builder says, helping him calculate load-bearing capacity for the fondant tiers. A surgeon and a soldier, engineering a cake at 11 PM.

An old army buddy finds @MessTinBakes on Instagram. DMs him: 'Suresh? Bundt cake wale Suresh?' Rawat's stomach drops. Then the next message: 'Bhai, meri beti ki shaadi hai. Cake order karna hai. Tujhe toh pata hai, tera chocolate cake Leh mein sabse achha tha.' He sits down. Reads it again. Types: 'Size batao.'
Rajan bites into a slice. Closes his eyes. 'Colonel sahab, desh ke liye ladna brave tha. Apron pehenke cake banana — woh toh aur bhi brave hai.'

episodes.synopsis: Colonel Suresh Rawat (retd.), bakes custom cakes from Second Shift's tiny kitchen. His army unit laughed when they found out. Now his cakes are at every Pune wedding.
episodes.caption: 28 years in the army. Now he wears a pink apron and pipes frosting at midnight. His old unit laughed. His old unit is now ordering wedding cakes. Bravery isn't always a battlefield.

episodes.title: On Air

slides.text: Ananya Deshmukh is a 22-year-old mass communication student at Fergusson College. She attends 70% of her lectures — just enough to keep her attendance. Her professors think she's average. Her internal marks are average. Everything about her academic life is aggressively average. That's by design.

'Suno Toh' — a podcast about ordinary people with extraordinary hidden lives. 38 episodes. 85,000 monthly listeners. She records, edits, and publishes everything herself. Her equipment is a Blue Yeti mic and Audacity. She's been doing this for two years. Her professors have no idea. Her listeners call her 'the voice.'

Her father is a retired postman. He told her stories every night — about the people on his route, their lives, their letters. 'Sabki kahani interesting hai, beta. Bas sunne wala chahiye.' She started the podcast to be that listener. The first episode had 12 listens. One of them was her father. He called and said, 'Yeh toh teri calling hai.'

Second Shift, Desk 2, every night. She edits here, records interviews here, plans here. She interviewed Farhan for episode 34 — 'The Auto Driver with 14 Scripts.' 14,000 listens. She interviewed Pratap for episode 36. She's basically documenting Second Shift without anyone realizing it's becoming a story.

Tonight, an email. A media production house in Mumbai. 'We love Suno Toh. We want to adapt it into a web series. Can we meet?' Ananya reads it four times. She's 22, sitting in a co-working space in Pune at 11 PM, and Mumbai wants her stories. She screenshots it. Sends it to one person: her father. He replies with a voice note. He's crying.

She tells Farhan. His face changes. 'Web series? Meri script bhi sun lo yaar.' She tells Meera. Meera says, 'Main host karungi.' She tells Vikram. 'I'll do the poster art.' By midnight, five Second Shifters are pitching ideas for a show that doesn't exist yet. But it feels like it already does.
Rajan listens from the counter. 'Sabki kahaani keh rahi hai. Par apni kahaani kaun sunayega?' He pours her chai. 'Episode 39 mein apne baare mein bhi baat kar.'

episodes.synopsis: Ananya Deshmukh, final year Fergusson College student, runs a podcast from Second Shift. More listeners than her professor's citations. Tonight, a media house comes calling.
episodes.caption: 85,000 listeners. A production house in Mumbai. And she's a 'below average' student according to her attendance register. Your transcript doesn't define your story. Who's listening to YOU?

episodes.title: Power and Peace

slides.text: A black sedan pulls up at 9 PM. A woman steps out — crisp cotton saree, government ID clipped to her bag, the posture of someone used to being listened to. Aditi Kulkarni, IAS, 2015 batch. Currently posted as sub-collector in Nashik. She's Rajan's daughter. And she's here to have a conversation she's been avoiding for two years.

'Papa, yeh kya hai?' She looks around. Desks, people working on laptops, someone painting, someone practicing music. 'Tum IAS the. Collector the. Secretary-level postings. Aur ab tum chai bana rahe ho?' Rajan pours her a cup. 'Pehle chai pi. Phir baat karte hain.'

'Papa, you had power. You could change policy, move files, build things. You had 200 people working under you. Now you have 15 desks and a chai counter.' Rajan sips his tea. 'Aditi, un 200 logon mein se kitne khush the?' She doesn't answer. 'Main 30 saal mein ek insaan ko bhi khush nahi kar paya. Yahan, roz 15 log khush jaate hain.'

'Chal, dikhaata hoon.' Rajan takes her around. 'Desk 4 — Meera. Banker. Stand-up comedian. Desk 7 — Vikram. CA. Painter. Desk 12 — Farhan. Auto driver. Screenwriter. Desk 11 — Pratap. Security guard. Learning to code.' Aditi watches. She sees the paintings, the scripts, the code, the chai cups. She sees people being themselves.

They pass Priya, mid-dance. Aditi stops. Watches. 'She's a software engineer,' Rajan says. 'She dances because her mother danced.' Aditi is quiet for a long time. Then: 'Mujhe bhi kuch karna tha, Papa. Photography. Remember? You said government job pehle.' Rajan's face changes. 'Haan. Maine kaha tha. Aur main galat tha.'

Aditi sits at an empty desk. Opens her phone. Her camera roll — hundreds of photos. Nashik at dawn, farmers in fog, children playing in government schools. All shot during her postings. Never shared. Rajan sits beside her. Looks at the photos. 'Beta, power thi. Peace nahi thi. Tujhe dono mil sakte hain. Yeh jagah tere liye bhi hai.'
Aditi leaves at midnight. At the door, she turns. 'Yeh space bachana, Papa. Main aaungi. Camera leke.' Rajan nods. Wipes the counter. His eyes are wet. He doesn't wipe those.

episodes.synopsis: Rajan's daughter Aditi, an IAS officer herself, visits Second Shift. She can't understand why her father left a position of power to make chai for strangers.
episodes.caption: 'Papa, you had power.' 'Beta, power thi. Peace nahi thi.' A father who built what he wished he'd had. A daughter who might finally use it. What would your parents say about YOUR second shift?

episodes.title: Rise and Fall

slides.text: A food blogger — 400K followers — walks into Second Shift at 10 PM. She smells the cake. 'Who's baking?' Colonel Rawat slides a slice across the counter. She takes one bite, pulls out her phone, and goes live. 'I just found the best cake in Pune and it's being made by a retired army colonel in a co-working space at midnight.' 50,000 views in two hours.

Three days later, a man in a suit walks in. He represents the building's landlord. 'You're running a commercial food operation from a co-working space. No food license. No FSSAI registration. No commercial kitchen permit. Shut it down or we'll file a complaint.' He leaves a legal notice on the counter. Rawat reads it. His hands don't shake — 28 years in the army taught him that.

The oven goes cold. Rawat stops baking. He comes to the space but just sits. Drinks chai. Meera tries a joke. He smiles, barely. Farhan says, 'Colonel sahab, mera ek script hai about an army cook. Read it?' Rawat says, 'Abhi nahi, beta.' The space feels different without the smell of cake.

Sunita walks up to Rawat's desk. 'Colonel sahab, FSSAI registration costs 2,000 rupees and takes two weeks. Cloud kitchen license — I checked — 5,000. Total investment: 7,000. Your monthly revenue is 1.5 lakhs.' She slides a paper across. It's a full business plan. The housewife trader just did his books.

Rohit the lawyer reviews the legal notice. 'This is a scare tactic.' Vikram designs a logo for @MessTinBakes. Ananya records a podcast episode. Pratap builds a basic website. In one night, Second Shift turns Colonel Rawat's hobby into a legal business.

Two weeks later, the oven is on again. FSSAI certificate framed on the wall next to a photo of Rawat's unit in Leh. First order as a legal business: a birthday cake. The customer's message: 'My son loves your cakes. He's in the army. Can you write "Happy Birthday Fauji" on it?' Rawat pipes the letters with the steadiest hands in Pune.
Rajan tastes the first legal slice. 'Colonel sahab, 30 saal army mein the. Ab community ne aapke liye ladai ladi. Bolo, kaisa laga?'

episodes.synopsis: Colonel Rawat's cakes go viral after a food blogger visits. But his old landlord sends a lawyer — he's been baking commercially without a food license. Sunita steps in with an unexpected solution.
episodes.caption: A food blogger made him viral. A lawyer tried to shut him down. His community built him a business in one night. That's what happens when your people have your back. Who's got YOUR back?

episodes.title: Two Stages

slides.text: An email at 3 PM during standup meeting. 'Dear Priya, we would like to invite you to perform at the Pune Cultural Festival.' A real stage. A real audience. This isn't a midnight practice session — this is the thing she's been working toward for two years. Her hands go cold in the middle of a Jira discussion.

The festival is Saturday. The product launch is Saturday. She's the lead developer. Six months of her code goes live that day. Her manager has already sent the calendar invite — 'Mandatory: All hands for launch.' Two stages. One person. Zero idea what to do.

At Second Shift, she asks everyone. Meera says, 'Dance. Your code doesn't need you on launch day.' Farhan says, 'Jab stage milta hai, ja.' Pratap says nothing. Then: 'Ma'am, aapne mujhe sikhaya ki koi bhi cheez start karne mein der nahi hoti. Toh kisi cheez ko choose karne mein bhi der nahi honi chahiye.'

She deploys the code Friday night. Tests everything twice. Leaves detailed documentation. Writes an email to her manager: 'Code is production-ready. Tests passing. I have a personal commitment Saturday afternoon. I'll be on call from 7 PM.' She doesn't explain. The code speaks for itself.

Saturday. 5 PM. Pune Cultural Festival. 200 people. Priya steps onto the stage wearing her mother's anklets. She dances for seven minutes. She makes one mistake — a slight stumble in the third sequence. She recovers. The audience doesn't notice. But she does. And she smiles. Because a year ago, she couldn't even do the first sequence.

At 7 PM, still in her dance saree, she opens her laptop backstage. The product launch went fine. Zero bugs. Her manager texts: 'Smooth launch. Where were you?' She sends a photo — her on stage. He doesn't reply for ten minutes. Then: 'Damn. Okay. Take Monday off.' She screams.
Rajan sees the photo on Ananya's story. Screenshots it. Puts it on the notice board. Writes: 'Yeh desk 8 ki Priya hai. Software engineer. Dancer. Dono.'

episodes.synopsis: Priya gets invited to perform Bharatanatyam at a cultural festival. But it's the same week as Infosys's biggest product launch. She has to choose — or does she?
episodes.caption: Her code launched without a single bug. Her dance had one stumble. She chose both stages. When you're forced to choose — what if the answer is 'both'?

episodes.title: Unmasked

slides.text: An email to the Neelkanth Instagram account: 'Dear Artist, Jehangir Art Gallery, Mumbai, would like to feature three of your works in our upcoming "New Voices" exhibition. We need your real name, bio, and a photograph. Please respond within one week.' Vikram reads it at his audit desk. His hands, still smelling of turpentine, are trembling.

'If they find out, I'm done.' He means his clients, his partners, his firm. CAs don't paint. CAs audit. The last time he mentioned art at work, a senior partner said, 'Vikram, creative hobbies are fine, but don't let them distract you from what matters.' What matters. He's been hearing that phrase his whole life.

At Second Shift, he tells the group. Meera says: 'Accept it. Are you insane?' Rohit says: 'I can review the gallery contract. Pro bono.' Kavya says, 'If you don't put your name on your art, the art stays safe but you stay invisible.' That one hits different.

He paints all night. A self-portrait — a man in a suit, tie loosened, one hand holding an audit file, the other holding a brush. Half the canvas is grey columns of numbers. Half is exploding color. The title: 'Neelkanth.' Blue-throated god. The one who swallowed poison so the world could live.

He calls the gallery on Friday night, from Second Shift. 'My name is Vikram Desai. I'm a chartered accountant at Deloitte. I'm Neelkanth.' Silence. Then: 'Mr. Desai, that makes the story even better. CA by day, artist by night. Is that okay?' He looks at Meera. She gives a thumbs up. 'Haan. That's who I am.'

Two weeks later, Jehangir Art Gallery. Three Neelkanth paintings on the wall. The self-portrait in the center. His firm's managing partner walks in. Sees him. 'Vikram?' Vikram stands straight. 'Sir. Welcome to my exhibition.' The partner stares at the self-portrait. Doesn't say 'what matters' this time.
Rajan wasn't at the gallery. But at Second Shift that night, Desk 7 has a small sign. Vikram finds it. Rajan's handwriting: 'Neelkanth ka asli desk. Painting chhupana band. Chai free hai aaj.'

episodes.synopsis: Vikram's anonymous art career hits a turning point — Jehangir Art Gallery wants to feature 'Neelkanth.' But they need a face. Vikram has to decide: stay hidden or step out.
episodes.caption: Jehangir Art Gallery. Three paintings. One chartered accountant. He swallowed the poison of hiding and finally let the art breathe. What's YOUR hidden name?

episodes.title: The Option

slides.text: Farhan's phone rings during a fare. Mumbai number. He pulls over. 'Mr. Sheikh? I heard your script on the Suno Toh podcast. We're interested.' Farhan sits in his auto, parked on Sinhagad Road, a Mumbai producer on the phone, and his meter still running.

Video call from Second Shift, Desk 12. The producer loves the script. 'One note — the auto driver character. Can we make him a software engineer? Auto drivers don't sell.' Farhan stares at the screen. The main character is him.

He talks to Meera. 'If I say yes, the script gets made. But it's not my story anymore.' Sunita says, 'Compromise is part of every deal. The question is — kitna compromise?' Rohit says, 'Counter-offer karo.'

Farhan calls back. 'Sir, the character stays an auto driver. That's the story. But I'll make you a deal — if the first 10 pages don't hook you, I'll rewrite it however you want.' The producer pauses. 'Send me the first 10 pages.'
Three days. Nothing. Day four, a WhatsApp message: 'Farhan bhai, the auto driver stays. When can we discuss the full script?' He pulls over. Same spot on Sinhagad Road. Same auto. Different man.

That night at Second Shift, Farhan walks in and goes to the whiteboard. Writes: 'SCRIPT #14 — SOLD.' The space erupts. Rawat brings cake. Meera starts a slow clap. Pratap whispers, 'Bhai, mere code ka naam credits mein daalna.' Farhan writes one more line: 'Auto driver hi rahega.'
Rajan raises a chai glass. 'Duniya kehti thi auto chalao. Usne kaha — auto waale ki kahaani sunao. Aur duniya ne suni.'

episodes.synopsis: A producer wants Farhan's screenplay but wants to change the auto driver to a software engineer. Farhan has to decide if the story matters more than the credit.
episodes.caption: They wanted to change his auto driver to a software engineer. He said no. The script sold anyway. Your story is only yours if you refuse to let them rewrite it.

episodes.title: Verse

slides.text: 1:15 AM. Most regulars have left. Rajan is cleaning up. A taxi stops outside. A man in an expensive overcoat walks in. 'Rajan.' 'Tripathi.' They stare at each other. Two men who shared an office in Mantralaya for five years.

'I read about this place on that podcast — Suno Toh. I didn't know it was yours.' Rajan pours chai. 'Toh batao, aadhi raat ko kyun aaye ho?' Tripathi pulls out a leather notebook. 'Mujhe bhi apna second shift chahiye.'

Urdu poetry. Pages and pages. Ghazals, nazms, couplets. Written in immaculate Nastaliq script. 20 years of hidden writing. 'Joint Secretary Tripathi writes Urdu shayari — can you imagine what the WhatsApp groups would say?' He laughs. It's a tired laugh.

Rajan says, 'Padho.' Tripathi reads. His voice cracks on the second couplet. It's about a man who builds walls all day and comes home to write about doors. Rajan listens. Doesn't interrupt. Just listens.

'Rajan, tum jab retire hue, maine socha — pagal hai. Ab samajh aaya. Tum free ho. Main abhi bhi yeh notebook chhupata hoon jaise contraband ho.' Rajan says, 'Toh mat chhupaao.' 'Itna easy nahi hai.' 'Kisi ne kaha easy hai?'

Tripathi tears a page from his notebook — the first time ever. Hands it to Rajan. It says: 'Jo din mein woh hain jo duniya chahti hai, raat mein woh hain jo khud chahte hain — aur raat zyada sachchi hai.' Rajan pins it to the notice board.
Rajan locks up at 3 AM. Looks at the notice board. A dancer's photo. An Urdu couplet. A painter's desk sign. He thinks: 'Yeh space deewarein nahi — darwaaze hai.' He turns off the lights.

episodes.synopsis: Rajan's former IAS colleague shows up at Second Shift at midnight. He writes Urdu poetry in secret. Even the powerful have things they hide.
episodes.caption: A joint secretary from Delhi. Urdu poetry hidden for 20 years. He came at 1 AM to read his first poem out loud. Even the powerful have secrets. 'Raat zyada sachchi hai.'

episodes.title: The Set

slides.text: Someone films Meera's set. Full video. Clear audio. Her face visible. '5 Reasons Why RBI Guidelines Are Funnier Than Your Tinder Bio.' 2.3 million views in four days. A talent manager DMs: 'We need to talk.'

The talent manager's pitch: shows, brand deals, possible Netflix audition. 'But Meera, this needs full commitment. You can't be a compliance officer at 9 AM and a comedian at 9 PM. Pick one.' She's heard this before. Her whole life has been about picking one thing.

She doesn't come to Second Shift for three nights. The banking salary pays her parents' medical bills. Her father's knee surgery is next month. Comedy doesn't have EMI-compatible income. She opens a spreadsheet — because of course a compliance officer makes a spreadsheet — and the numbers don't lie.

Night four. Back at Desk 4. Sunita walks over. Listens. Then: 'Tu bank mat chhod. Main tere comedy income ka portfolio manage karungi. Pehle part-time. Phir jab numbers match karein — full-time. Main numbers jaanti hoon, Meera. Trust me.'

Meera calls the talent manager. 'I'm in. But I keep my bank job for now. If you want someone who's funny AND has a spreadsheet for her five-year plan — main hoon na.' The manager laughs. 'You're already doing a bit. Fine. Deal.'

First managed show. 200 people. Still in her office kurti. 'Hi, I'm Meera. By day I approve your home loans. By night I roast you for needing them.' The crowd loses it. Backstage, she texts Second Shift group: 'Pehla paid show done. Kal chai meri taraf se.'
Rajan reads the group chat. Types slowly: 'Desk 4 ka rate badh gaya. Celebrity surcharge.' Then: 'Mazaak hai. Chai humesha free hai.'

episodes.synopsis: Meera's stand-up goes viral — 2.3 million views. A talent manager offers representation but wants her full-time. Sunita helps her build a bridge instead of burning one.
episodes.caption: 2.3 million views. A talent offer. She said: 'Not yet. But soon.' Sometimes the bravest thing isn't quitting — it's building the bridge while you're still on it.

episodes.title: The Resume

slides.text: Pratap fills out a job application on Naukri. Education: 12th pass, Beed. Work experience: Security Guard, 3 years. Skills: Python, HTML/CSS, Problem solving. His resume fits in three lines. The other applicants probably have degrees longer than his entire CV.

Priya rewrites his resume. Removes nothing. Adds what matters. 'Self-taught Python developer. 3 projects. Active GitHub with daily commits for 4 months.' Below work experience: 'Learned to code while working 12-hour security shifts. Every skill on this resume was built between 11 PM and 2 AM.'

A Baner startup calls. The interviewer is 26. 'So you're... a security guard?' 'Haan.' 'And you learned coding at night?' 'Haan, 11 PM to 2 AM.' 'Why?' 'Kyunki 7 AM to 7 PM mein main gate kholne mein busy tha. Par raat mein main apna gate khud kholta hoon.'
'Write a function that reverses a string.' 30 seconds. Done. Harder problem. Gets stuck. Tries. Gets 80%. Says honestly: 'Yahan tak aata hai mujhe. Baaki seekh lunga.'

Two days later. 2 PM. Pratap at Gate 3, lifting the barrier. 'We'd like to offer you the internship. 15,000 per month.' He sits on the pavement. Calls Priya. Can't speak for ten seconds. She says, 'Tu roya na? Chal, raat ko cake khate hain.'

Last night at Second Shift as a security guard. Types print('hello world') one more time. Farhan sits next to him. 'Tera growth mere se zyada fast hai, yaar.' They laugh. He saves the file: 'first_and_last_hello_world.py'
Rajan puts a nameplate on Desk 11: 'Pratap Gaikwad. Developer. (Pehle Gate 3.)' Pratap says, 'Gate 3 hatao.' Rajan says, 'Kabhi nahi. Yeh tera origin story hai.'

episodes.synopsis: Pratap applies for a junior developer internship. His resume has 'Security Guard' as his only experience. His GitHub tells a different story.
episodes.caption: 'Security Guard' was his only experience. His GitHub had 4 months of daily commits. The startup hired a developer who learns at midnight. What are you building at midnight?

episodes.title: The Portfolio

slides.text: Sunday morning. Sunita's phone charging in the kitchen. Her husband picks it up for Swiggy. A notification: 'Zerodha: Your portfolio is up 3.2% this week.' He opens the app. 8.7 lakhs. Opens 'Recipes' folder. It's not recipes.
He doesn't say anything at breakfast. Or lunch. Sunita notices the silence. By evening, she checks her phone. The Zerodha notification was opened. Her stomach drops.

After the kids sleep. 'Zerodha? Since when?' '11 months.' 'How much?' '50,000 start. 8.7 lakhs now.' He's quiet. 'Mera financial advisor ne 3 saal mein 6 lakh banaye. Tumne 11 mahine mein 8.7?' She nods. He sits down. She waits for anger. It doesn't come.

'Main gussa nahi hoon. Main sharminda hoon. Maine dinner party pe kaha tha ki tum paise samajhti nahi. Ussi raat se, na?' She nods. 'Mujhe bataya kyun nahi?' 'Kyunki tumne kabhi pucha nahi ki main kya karti hoon ek baje tak jaag ke.' That lands.

'Teach me.' She laughs. He's serious. 'Agar meri wife itni achhi trader hai toh main kyun 1% FD mein paisa daal raha hoon?' She opens Zerodha. Shows him charts. At 11 PM. On their sofa. She's doing her second shift at home.

Next night at Second Shift, Sunita walks in to Desk 9. Farhan asks, 'Sab theek?' She smiles. 'Mera husband ne mujhe ek aur 50,000 diye hain. Invest karne ke liye.' The space cheers. The 'Recipes' folder has been renamed. It just says 'Portfolio.'
Rajan pours her chai. 'Sunita ji, pati ko bhi lao kabhi.' She says, 'Usse bhi desk chahiye?' Rajan says, 'Haan. Par uska second shift hoga — apni wife ko samajhna.'

episodes.synopsis: Sunita's husband finds Zerodha, the 'Recipes' folder, the 8.7 lakhs. The secret is out. But the conversation isn't what anyone expected.
episodes.caption: She hid 8.7 lakhs in a folder called 'Recipes.' He found out. Instead of anger — 'Teach me.' The real bull run isn't in the market. It's when someone finally sees you.

episodes.title: Ink and Identity

slides.text: One photo. KR Ink's Instagram — close-up of Kavya's hands tattooing. Professional, anonymous. Except her wrist: the TechMahindra wellness band. Corporate blue. Logo visible. A marketing colleague noticed. Screenshotted. 'Is this one of ours?'
Monday. The air feels different. Whispers. Manager calls 11 AM meeting. She texts Second Shift group: 'I think I'm done. They found out.' Meera replies: 'Breathe. We're here.'
'Kavya, is this you?' She could deny it. But she's tired of hiding. 'Haan. That's me. I'm KR Ink.'

Her manager: 'One — you're in violation of your own policy. Two — 14 people in this office have asked if KR Ink does walk-ins. Including the VP of Engineering.' He pauses. 'Maybe it's time we update the policy. Since the person who wrote it clearly disagrees with it.'

That afternoon, Kavya rewrites the dress code. New version: 'TechMahindra respects individual expression. Visible tattoos are permitted.' Approved in 12 minutes. She rolls up her sleeves at her desk. For the first time in four years.

That night at Second Shift, sleeves rolled up. No blazer. The space erupts. Vikram says, 'Welcome to the people who stopped hiding club.' First client of the night: her own manager. He wants one word on his wrist: 'Update.'
Rajan looks at his 'Permission' tattoo. Looks at Kavya's arms. 'Tumne toh poori company ko permission de di.'

episodes.synopsis: Kavya's double life as a tattoo artist is exposed when a colleague spots her corporate wellness band in a KR Ink photo. But the fallout is not what she expected.
episodes.caption: She wrote the dress code. She violated it. She rewrote it. Sometimes the rules need changing by the person who broke them first.

episodes.title: The Space

slides.text: A letter on the counter. Rent increased to 2,40,000. 'Please confirm or vacate within 30 days.' Rajan reads it. Folds it neatly. Places it under the chai counter. Pours himself a cup. Drinks it alone.
He doesn't tell anyone for three days. Then Sunita checks the UPI account. The math doesn't work. 'Rajan uncle, kitna badhaya hai?'
Midnight. Full group. Everyone's here. Even Aditi on video from Nashik. Rajan stands behind the counter. 'Space band ho raha hai. Rent double ho gaya. Main afford nahi kar sakta.'

Sunita: 'Subscription model. 15 regulars at 5,000 each.' Rohit: 'That rent increase isn't legal without 90-day notice.' Ananya: 'Fundraiser podcast episode. 85,000 listeners.' Vikram: 'I'll sell three paintings.' One by one. Everyone has a piece.

Farhan takes the marker. Writes: 'SAVE SECOND SHIFT.' Meera: benefit show. Kavya: tattoo marathon. Pratap: 'Meri pehli salary aayi hai. 5,000 deta hoon.' Priya: paid coding workshops. Rawat: 20% of cake orders. The whiteboard fills up.

Rajan looks at each person. The banker-comedian. The CA-painter. The auto-driver-screenwriter. The housewife-trader. The security-guard-developer. All of them. Here. Fighting for a space that gave them permission to be whole. He built it for them. They're saving it for him.

Rajan stands up. Looks at his wrist. 'Permission.' Looks at the room. 'Maine yeh jagah banayi thi taaki log woh kar sakein jo karna chahte hain.' He pauses. 'Pata nahi tha ki woh mujhe bhi bachayenge.' He pours chai. One cup at a time. Fifteen cups. The space isn't shutting down. The second shift continues.

episodes.synopsis: The landlord doubles rent. Second Shift can't survive. Rajan is ready to close. But the regulars have a different plan. The space was never about desks — it was about permission.
episodes.caption: They came for desks. They stayed for permission. When the space almost died, they saved it — because Second Shift was never about a co-working space. It was about being allowed to be more than one thing. Your day job pays the bills. Your second shift pays the soul. See you after 6.
